pos: v. (third person singular of ail: to trouble, afflict; in the AV only in the question What aileth thee?, rendering the Hebrew idiom mah-lak, what is to thee)
etymology: Old English eglan, to trouble, pain. The Hebrew has no verb behind it; the question is literally “what to thee?” — what is the matter.
biblical_def: The angel of God to Hagar in the wilderness: “What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is” (Gen 21:17). The king to the woman of Tekoah: “What aileth thee? And she answered, I am indeed a widow woman” (2Sa 14:5). The king of Israel to the mother on the wall of Samaria: “What aileth thee? And she answered, This woman said unto me, Give thy son, that we may eat him” (2Ki 6:28). Saul coming from the field: “What aileth the people that they weep?” (1Sa 11:5). Isaiah to Jerusalem: “What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?” (Isa 22:1). And the psalm to the Red Sea: “What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest?” (Psa 114:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ail as to trouble, to affect with pain or uneasiness; used only of some slight or uncertain disorder: what aileth him?
webster_full: AIL, v.t. To trouble; to affect with pain or uneasiness, either of body or mind; used to express some uneasiness or affection, whose cause is unknown; as, what ails the man? I know not what ails him.
scriptures: And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.
And the king said unto her, What aileth thee? And she answered, I am indeed a widow woman, and mine husband is dead.
And the king said unto her, What aileth thee? And she answered, This woman said unto me, Give thy son, that we may eat him to day, and we will eat my son to morrow.
Isa 22:1
The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?
What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back?
corruption_summary: God's question to Hagar is read as God finding something out, when every question God asks in Scripture is asked for the hearer's sake.
corruption_paragraphs: “What aileth thee, Hagar?” is asked by the One who, in the same sentence, says He has already heard the boy. God asked Adam where he was, Cain where his brother was, and Hagar what ailed her, and in none of the three did He lack the information. The question is an invitation to say the thing aloud to the One who can answer it, and Hagar's answer — a slave girl's cry over a dying child — opened the well she had not seen. Prayer does not inform God; it brings the ailing thing into His hearing, where He has been the whole time. Psalm 114 turns the question on the sea and the mountains, and they have no answer, because the answer is the presence of the Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew mah-lak (H4100), what is to thee, what is the matter with thee; the AV's aileth supplies the verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew mah-lak (H4100 with a pronominal suffix) — what to thee; Genesis 21:17, Judges 18:23–24, 1 Samuel 11:5, 2 Samuel 14:5, 2 Kings 6:28, Isaiah 22:1, Psalm 114:5.
usage: “What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not” — asked by the One who had already heard.
“What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest?” — the question creation cannot answer.
“What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?” — Isaiah to a city in panic.

pos: adv. (at a distance within view; over there; rendering Hebrew koh and Greek ekei)
etymology: Old English geond, through, beyond. The word points; it is spoken by a man who can see the place he means and is about to go to it.
biblical_def: Abraham at the foot of Moriah: “Abide ye here with the ass; and I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you” (Gen 22:5). The Lord at Gethsemane: “Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder” (Mat 26:36). Balaam to Balak: “Stand here by thy burnt offering, while I meet the LORD yonder” (Num 23:15). Elisha seeing the Shunammite: “Behold, yonder is that Shunammite” (2Ki 4:25). And of faith: “If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove” (Mat 17:20). Reuben and Gad would not inherit “on yonder side Jordan” (Num 32:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines yonder as at a distance within view.
webster_full: YONDER, a. Being at a distance within view; as yonder hill.
YONDER, adv. At a distance within view.
scriptures: Gen 22:5
And Abraham said unto his young men, Abide ye here with the ass; and I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you.
Then cometh Jesus with them unto a place called Gethsemane, and saith unto the disciples, Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder.
And he said unto Balak, Stand here by thy burnt offering, while I meet the LORD yonder.

And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you.
So she went and came unto the man of God to mount Carmel. And it came to pass, when the man of God saw her afar off, that he said to Gehazi his servant, Behold, yonder is that Shunammite:
corruption_summary: Abraham's come again to you is read as a kind lie to the servants, and Hebrews says it was the arithmetic of the resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 22:5 is often read as a father sparing his servants the truth. Abraham said we will go yonder and worship, and we will come again — carrying the knife and the fire and the boy who was to be the sacrifice — and Hebrews 11:19 gives the plain reading: he accounted that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead. The father who went yonder expected to come back with the son, by resurrection if by nothing else, because the promise was in that son and the promise could not fail. Two thousand years later another Son said to His disciples, “Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder,” and went a stone's cast further into the same obedience; and He too came again to them. Yonder in Scripture is where a man goes alone to worship with a knife at his side, and it is not the end of the story.
roots_summary: Hebrew koh (H3541), thus, here, there, yonder; Greek ekei (G1563), there, in that place.
roots_lines: Hebrew ad-koh (H3541) — as far as yonder; Genesis 22:5; koh, Numbers 23:15; halom (H1973), Numbers 16:37.
Greek ekei (G1563) — there, yonder; Matthew 17:20, 26:36.
usage: “I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you” — the resurrection counted on before it happened.
“Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder” — the Son on His Moriah.
“Remove hence to yonder place” — faith as a grain of mustard seed.

pos: n. (an instrument for writing; a stylus; rendering Hebrew et, cheret, and shebet, Greek kalamos)
etymology: Latin penna, a feather. The Hebrew et is an iron stylus for tablets and rock; the Greek kalamos a reed cut for ink.
biblical_def: The sons of Korah: “My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer” (Psa 45:1). Jeremiah against the scribes: “How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain” (Jer 8:8); and of the nation: “The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond” (Jer 17:1). Job wished his words “graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever” (Job 19:24). Isaiah was told to “write in it with a man's pen” (Isa 8:1). Deborah's song names “they that handle the pen of the writer” (Jdg 5:14). John: “I will not with ink and pen write unto thee” (3Jn 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pen as an instrument used for writing, usually made of the quill of some large fowl; also, a stylus.
webster_full: PEN, n. An instrument used for writing, usually made of the quill of some large fowl, but it may be of any other material.
2. A writer; a person that writes; as, an able pen.
PEN, n. A small inclosure for beasts, as for cows or sheep.
scriptures: Psa 45:1

To the chief Musician upon Shoshannim, for the sons of Korah, Maschil, A Song of loves. My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.
Jer 8:8
How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain.
Jer 17:1
The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars;
That they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever!
I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee:
corruption_summary: The writers of Scripture are treated as its authors, and the psalmist called his own tongue the pen of a ready writer.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 45:1 is the Bible's own picture of inspiration. The psalmist's heart is full, his tongue is moving, and he calls that tongue a pen — the instrument, not the writer. The pen has its own shape and leaves its own mark; David does not write like Isaiah, and Luke does not write like John; but a pen does not compose. The higher critic reads the Psalms as the religious feelings of ancient poets, and Peter answers that holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. Jeremiah 8:8 is the other pen: scribes who had the law of the LORD in their hands and made it lie, so that the pen itself was in vain. A pen in the wrong hand can falsify what it copies, and a pen in the right hand is Scripture.
roots_summary: Hebrew et (H5842), a stylus, iron pen; cheret (H2747), a graving tool; shebet (H7626), a rod, staff; Greek kalamos (G2563), a reed.
roots_lines: Hebrew et (H5842) — a stylus, pen; Psalm 45:1, Job 19:24, Jeremiah 8:8, 17:1.
Hebrew cheret (H2747) — a graving tool; Isaiah 8:1, Exodus 32:4; shebet (H7626), the writer's staff; Judges 5:14.
Greek kalamos (G2563) — a reed, reed pen; 3 John 1:13, Matthew 11:7.
usage: “My tongue is the pen of a ready writer” — the instrument, not the author.
“The pen of the scribes is in vain” — the law in hand and falsified.
“Written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond” — Judah's sin engraved.

pos: n. (the visible heaven; the region of clouds; rendering Hebrew shachaq, Greek ouranos)
etymology: Old Norse sky, a cloud. The Hebrew shachaq is the fine dust of the upper air, the clouds; the English word once meant the cloud itself before it meant the space the cloud is in.
biblical_def: The Lord to the Pharisees: “When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red. And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?” (Mat 16:2–3; Luk 12:56). Elihu to Job: “Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass?” (Job 37:18). Moses' blessing: “who rideth upon the heaven in thy help, and in his excellency on the sky” (Deu 33:26). And of Abraham's seed: “so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable” (Heb 11:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sky as the aerial region which surrounds the earth; the apparent arch or vault of heaven; the heavens.
webster_full: SKY, n. The aerial region which surrounds the earth; the apparent arch or vault of heaven, which in a clear day is of a blue color.
2. The heavens.
3. The weather; the climate.
scriptures: Mat 16:3
And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?
Mat 16:2
He answered and said unto them, When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red.
Ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky and of the earth; but how is it that ye do not discern this time?
Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass?
There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy help, and in his excellency on the sky.
Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable.
corruption_summary: A generation expert in forecasting reads the sky and cannot read the times, which is the Lord's exact charge against the Pharisees.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 16:3 describes an age that can predict the weather and not the judgment. The Pharisees had a working science of the red sky and no eye for the Messiah standing in front of them, and the Lord's word for that is not ignorance but hypocrisy — the skill was real, and it was applied to the sky and withheld from the times. The modern world reads its markets, its models, and its forecasts with great care and is unable to see that the signs the prophets gave have been fulfilled in a Man. Job 37:18 is the older correction: the sky is spread out by Someone, strong and as a molten looking glass, and the man who studies it and does not see the hand that stretched it has looked at the glass and missed the reflection.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachaq (H7834), a cloud, the fine dust of the sky; Greek ouranos (G3772), heaven, sky.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachaq (H7834) — cloud, sky, the skies; Deuteronomy 33:26, Job 37:18, Psalm 18:11, 77:17, Isaiah 45:8, Jeremiah 51:9.
Greek ouranos (G3772) — heaven, sky; Matthew 16:2–3, Luke 12:56, Hebrews 11:12.
usage: “Ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?” — skill in the wrong direction.
“Spread out the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass” — Elihu's question.
“As the stars of the sky in multitude” — the promise's arithmetic.

pos: adj. and adv. (yielding, gentle, tender; rendering Hebrew rak, rakak, and at, Greek malakos)
etymology: Old English sōfte, gentle, easy. The Greek malakos is the same word the AV renders effeminate in 1 Corinthians 6:9 — soft of clothing in one place, soft of men in another.
biblical_def: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger” (Pro 15:1). “By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone” (Pro 25:15). Job: “For God maketh my heart soft, and the Almighty troubleth me” (Job 23:16). Of leviathan: “will he speak soft words unto thee?” (Job 41:3). The Lord of John: “they that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses” (Mat 11:8). Adverbially: Jacob would “lead on softly” (Gen 33:14); Ahab “went softly” in sackcloth (1Ki 21:27); “the waters of Shiloah that go softly” were refused for the river (Isa 8:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines soft as easily yielding to pressure; not hard; mild; gentle; smooth; effeminate; not manly.
webster_full: SOFT, a. Easily yielding to pressure; the contrary of hard; as a soft bed; soft clay.
2. Not rough or harsh; gentle to the touch; delicate; smooth.
3. Mild; gentle; kind; not severe or unfeeling; as a soft answer.
4. Effeminate; viciously nice; not manly.
scriptures: Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone.
For God maketh my heart soft, and the Almighty troubleth me:
Mat 11:8
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? behold, they that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses.
Isa 8:6
Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son;
And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly.
corruption_summary: A soft answer is confused with a spineless one, and the same proverb says the soft tongue breaks bone.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 15:1 is quoted to recommend saying nothing, and Proverbs 25:15 sits ten chapters away to explain that a soft tongue is not a silent one: it breaketh the bone. The softness Solomon commends is gentleness that gets through, the word that turns wrath rather than feeding it and persuades a prince rather than defying him — a strength under control, not an absence of it. Scripture has the other softness too, and names it without kindness: the men in soft clothing in kings' houses whom John was not one of, and the malakoi of 1 Corinthians 6 who shall not inherit the kingdom, where the AV's word is effeminate. Softness of speech is a grace; softness of manhood is listed with the sins. Job 23:16 knows a third softness, the only one that saves: God maketh my heart soft — the hardness taken out by trouble, so that the man can feel the hand on him.
roots_summary: Hebrew rak (H7390), tender, soft; rakak (H7401), to be soft, faint; at (H328), gently, softly; Greek malakos (G3120), soft, effeminate.
roots_lines: Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft; Proverbs 15:1, 25:15, Job 41:3, Deuteronomy 28:54.
Hebrew rakak (H7401) — to be soft, tender; Job 23:16; at (H328), softly, gently; Genesis 33:14, 1 Kings 21:27, Isaiah 8:6.
Greek malakos (G3120) — soft; Matthew 11:8, Luke 7:25; rendered effeminate in 1 Corinthians 6:9.
usage: “A soft answer turneth away wrath” — and a soft tongue breaketh the bone.
“They that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses” — John was not among them.
“God maketh my heart soft” — the softening that trouble does.

pos: v. (to illuminate; to make less heavy; rendering Hebrew or, nagah, and qalal, Greek photizo and apokalupsis)
etymology: Two English words of different descent share the form: from light the illumination, and from light the opposite of heavy. The Authorized Version uses both.
biblical_def: Simeon's song: “A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel” (Luk 2:32). David: “lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death” (Psa 13:3); “the LORD will lighten my darkness” (2Sa 22:29). The city that needs no sun: “the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof” (Rev 21:23). Ezra: God has given a little reviving, “to lighten our eyes” (Ezr 9:8). In the other sense, Jonah's sailors “cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them” (Jon 1:5), and the Philistine priests hoped God would “lighten his hand from off you” (1Sa 6:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lighten as to illuminate, to fill with light; and, as a second word, to make lighter, to reduce in weight, to alleviate.
webster_full: LIGHTEN, v.t. To dissipate darkness; to fill with light; to spread over with light; to illuminate.
2. To illuminate with knowledge.
LIGHTEN, v.t. To make lighter; to reduce in weight; to make less heavy.
2. To alleviate; to make less burdensome or afflictive.
scriptures: Luk 2:32
A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.
Psa 13:3
Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death;
And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.
Jon 1:5

Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
For thou art my lamp, O LORD: and the LORD will lighten my darkness.

Wherefore ye shall make images of your emerods, and images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel: peradventure he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land.
corruption_summary: Ministries lighten the load by throwing the cargo overboard, and the only lightening Scripture praises is the light in the eyes.
corruption_paragraphs: Jonah's sailors lightened the ship by casting the wares into the sea, and it did nothing, because the weight was a sleeping prophet in the hold. The church has its own version of the manoeuvre: when the storm comes, throw doctrine overboard — the hard sayings, the hell, the wrath, the exclusivity of Christ — and the ship rides no higher, because the weight was never the cargo. The other lightening is what Scripture asks for: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death; a light to lighten the Gentiles. Simeon's Greek is apokalupsis, a revelation — the child in his arms was light for the unveiling of the nations, and the city at the end has no sun because the glory of God lightens it. Lightening in the Bible is something done to eyes, not to loads.
roots_summary: Hebrew or (H215), to give light; nagah (H5050), to shine; qalal (H7043), to make light, lessen; Greek photizo (G5461), to illuminate; apokalupsis (G602), an unveiling.
roots_lines: Hebrew or, hiphil (H215) — to give light, lighten; Psalm 13:3, Ezra 9:8; nagah (H5050), 2 Samuel 22:29.
Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to lighten, make light; 1 Samuel 6:5, Jonah 1:5.
Greek photizo (G5461) — to illuminate; Revelation 21:23; apokalupsis (G602), revelation; Luke 2:32, “to lighten the Gentiles.”
usage: “A light to lighten the Gentiles” — Simeon's revelation.
“Lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death” — David's prayer.
“Cast forth the wares… to lighten it of them” — the cargo overboard, the weight still in the hold.

pos: adv. (without doubt, certainly; rendering the Hebrew oath-formula and infinitive absolute, Greek menounge and ge)
etymology: Doubt + less: free of doubt. The Hebrew has no such adverb; the AV supplies it where the Hebrew doubles a verb or swears an oath.
biblical_def: Paul: “Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Php 3:8). The psalm of the sower: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him” (Psa 126:6). Isaiah's prayer: “Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us” (Isa 63:16). The LORD's oath in the wilderness: “Doubtless ye shall not come into the land… save Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun” (Num 14:30). Paul to Corinth: “If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you” (1Co 9:2). David enquiring: “Go up: for I will doubtless deliver the Philistines into thine hand” (2Sa 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doubtless as without doubt or question; unquestionably.
webster_full: DOUBTLESS, a. Free from fear or danger; secure.
DOUBTLESS, adv. Without doubt or question; unquestionably.
scriptures: Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not: thou, O LORD, art our father, our redeemer; thy name is from everlasting.
Doubtless ye shall not come into the land, concerning which I sware to make you dwell therein, save Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.
If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord.
corruption_summary: Doubt is praised as honesty and certainty suspected as pride, and the Bible's doubtless is spoken by God, by a sower, and by an apostle counting his losses.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has made a virtue of not being sure. Scripture's doubtless is not the confidence of a man who has never questioned; it is the settled end of a question. Paul's “yea doubtless” comes after he has laid every credential on the table and moved the column; the sower's “shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” is said of a man who went out weeping; Isaiah's “doubtless thou art our father” is prayed by a people whom Abraham would not recognise. Certainty in the Bible is reached through the tears, not around them, and it is not humility to stop short of it. Numbers 14:30 shows the other side: God's doubtless. The oath that the generation would not enter the land was as certain as the promise that Caleb would, and both were kept to the man.
roots_summary: Hebrew infinitive absolute (bo yabo, coming he shall come) and the oath-formula im (H518); Greek menounge (G3304), yea rather, doubtless; ge (G1065), at least, indeed.
roots_lines: Hebrew bo yabo (H935 doubled) — he shall surely come; Psalm 126:6; im (H518) in an oath, “doubtless ye shall not”; Numbers 14:30; ki (H3588), Isaiah 63:16.
Greek menounge (G3304) — yea doubtless; Philippians 3:8; ge (G1065), 1 Corinthians 9:2.
usage: “Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss” — certainty after the reckoning.
“Shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” — said of a man who went out weeping.
“Doubtless ye shall not come into the land” — God's certainty, kept to the man.

pos: v. (asked with authority; questioned; rendering Hebrew sha'al, Aramaic she'el, Greek punthanomai and eperotao)
etymology: Latin demandare, to entrust, through Old French demander, to ask. In the AV the word is a question put by a superior — a king, a captain, or God.
biblical_def: God out of the whirlwind: “Gird up now thy loins like a man; for I will demand of thee, and answer thou me” (Job 38:3; 40:7), and Job at the end: “I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me” (Job 42:4). Herod “demanded of them where Christ should be born” (Mat 2:4). The soldiers “demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do?” (Luk 3:14). The Lord “was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come” (Luk 17:20). Nebuchadnezzar's secret “which the king hath demanded” no wise man could show (Dan 2:27). David “demanded of” Uriah how the war went (2Sa 11:7). The chief captain “demanded who he was, and what he had done” (Act 21:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines demand as to ask or call for as one who has a claim or right; to require; to ask by authority; to question.
webster_full: DEMAND, v.t. To ask or call for, as one who has a claim or right to receive what is sought.
2. To require as necessary or useful.
3. To ask by authority; to question; to interrogate.
scriptures: Job 38:3
Gird up now thy loins like a man; for I will demand of thee, and answer thou me.
Job 42:4
Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me.
Mat 2:4
And when he had gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people together, he demanded of them where Christ should be born.
Luk 3:14
And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
And when he was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come, he answered them and said, The kingdom of God cometh not with observation:
Dan 2:27
Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said, The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king;
corruption_summary: Man demands of God and calls it honest wrestling, and the book of Job ends with God demanding of man and man putting his hand on his mouth.
corruption_paragraphs: Job spent thirty chapters demanding an audience — “Oh that I knew where I might find him!… I would order my cause before him” — and when the audience came, the first words out of the whirlwind reversed the courtroom: I will demand of thee, and answer thou me. What followed was not an explanation of Job's sufferings but seventy questions about the foundations of the earth, and Job's reply was a hand on his mouth. The modern posture of demanding an account from God is admired as authenticity; the book that gives it the fullest hearing ends by turning the demand round. Herod's demand is the other warning: he asked the right question of the right people and got the right answer — Bethlehem — and used it to plan a massacre. A correct answer demanded for a wrong reason is worse than ignorance.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'al (H7592), to ask, enquire, demand; Aramaic she'el (H7593), to ask; Greek punthanomai (G4441), to enquire; eperotao (G1905), to question.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask, demand; Job 38:3, 40:7, 42:4, 2 Samuel 11:7; Aramaic she'el (H7593), Daniel 2:27.
Greek punthanomai (G4441) — to enquire, demand; Matthew 2:4, Acts 21:33; eperotao (G1905), Luke 3:14, 17:20.
usage: “I will demand of thee, and answer thou me” — the courtroom reversed.
“Demanded of them where Christ should be born” — the right answer for a massacre.
“The soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do?” — an honest demand, honestly answered.

pos: n. and v. (knowledge joined to ability; to know how; rendering Hebrew sakal, yada, and bin)
etymology: Old Norse skil, discernment, distinction. The AV also keeps the old verb: Hiram's men can skill to hew timber — they know how.
biblical_def: Of Daniel and his friends: “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17); and Gabriel to Daniel: “I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding” (Dan 9:22). Solomon to Hiram: “there is not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians” (1Ki 5:6); “I know that thy servants can skill to cut timber in Lebanon” (2Ch 2:8). The overseers of Josiah's repairs were Levites, “all that could skill of instruments of musick” (2Ch 34:12). And the Preacher: “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecc 9:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines skill as the familiar knowledge of any art or science, united with readiness and dexterity in execution; and, as a verb, to know, to understand.
webster_full: SKILL, n. The familiar knowledge of any art or science, united with readiness and dexterity in execution or performance, or in the application of the art or science to practical purposes.
2. Knowledge; understanding.
SKILL, v.i. To know; to understand; to be knowing in. Obsolete.
scriptures: Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Dan 9:22
And he informed me, and talked with me, and said, O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding.

Now therefore command thou that they hew me cedar trees out of Lebanon; and my servants shall be with thy servants: and unto thee will I give hire for thy servants according to all that thou shalt appoint: for thou knowest that there is not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians.

And the men did the work faithfully: and the overseers of them were Jahath and Obadiah, the Levites, of the sons of Merari; and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to set it forward; and other of the Levites, all that could skill of instruments of musick.
Ecc 9:11

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
corruption_summary: Skill is either despised in the church as worldly or trusted as sufficient, and Daniel's was given by God and Ecclesiastes says it guarantees nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Two churches misuse the word. One treats skill as carnal — the preacher should not prepare, the musician should not practise, the builder should not be a Sidonian — and Solomon sent to Hiram for men who could skill to hew timber because there were none in Israel, and God filled Bezaleel with wisdom in every manner of workmanship for the tabernacle. The other church trusts skill outright, and Ecclesiastes 9:11 is written for it: favour is not to men of skill, time and chance happen to them all, and the most competent ministry in the country can fail while a stammerer is used. Daniel 1:17 holds the two together in one sentence: God gave them skill. It was real skill, it was studied for three years in a pagan school, and it was a gift.
roots_summary: Hebrew sakal (H7919), to be prudent, act wisely, give skill; yada (H3045), to know, know how; bin (H995), to discern, be skilled in.
roots_lines: Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to have insight, skill; Daniel 1:17, 9:22, 1 Samuel 18:14.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know how, can skill; 1 Kings 5:6, 2 Chronicles 2:7–8, Ecclesiastes 9:11.
Hebrew bin (H995) — to be skilled, discerning; 2 Chronicles 34:12, Daniel 1:20.
usage: “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” — studied for three years, and a gift.
“Not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians” — the temple built with pagan craft.
“Nor yet favour to men of skill” — the Preacher's limit.

pos: adj. and v. (in the AV, careless, free from anxiety, unguarded; to make free from care; rendering Hebrew batach, Greek amerimnos)
etymology: Latin securus, se + cura, without care. The Authorized Version keeps the Latin sense: to be secure is not to be safe but to feel safe, and in Judges 18 the two come apart.
biblical_def: The Danite spies found Laish “how they dwelt careless, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure” (Jdg 18:7), reported “ye shall come unto a people secure, and to a large land” (Jdg 18:10), and destroyed it. Job: “The tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure” (Job 12:6). Zophar's promise: “thou shalt be secure, because there is hope” (Job 11:18). Gideon smote the host of Midian “for the host was secure” (Jdg 8:11). The chief priests to the soldiers: “if this come to the governor's ears, we will persuade him, and secure you” (Mat 28:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines secure as free from fear or apprehension of danger; careless; confident; also safe; and, as a verb, to make safe, to guard.
webster_full: SECURE, a. Free from fear or apprehension of danger; not alarmed; not disturbed by fear; confident of safety; hence, careless of the means of defense.
2. Confident; not distrustful.
3. Free from danger; safe.
SECURE, v.t. To guard effectually from danger; to make safe.
scriptures: Jdg 18:7

Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people that were therein, how they dwelt careless, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure; and there was no magistrate in the land, that might put them to shame in any thing; and they were far from the Zidonians, and had no business with any man.
When ye go, ye shall come unto a people secure, and to a large land: for God hath given it into your hands; a place where there is no want of any thing that is in the earth.
Job 12:6
The tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure; into whose hand God bringeth abundantly.
And thou shalt be secure, because there is hope; yea, thou shalt dig about thee, and thou shalt take thy rest in safety.
And if this come to the governor's ears, we will persuade him, and secure you.
corruption_summary: The AV's secure means careless, and the carnal security of Laish is the security most congregations mean when they use the word.
corruption_paragraphs: When the Authorized Version calls a people secure it is describing their feelings, not their situation. Laish was quiet and secure and had no deliverer; the host of Midian was secure and Gideon was in the camp; they that provoke God are secure, says Job, and prosper, and the whole point is that the feeling and the fact are opposite. The old divines called this carnal security — the peace of a man who has not been disturbed by God — and preached against it as the most dangerous condition a soul could be in, because it is the one condition that does not know it needs anything. The Reformed doctrine of eternal security is a different word in a different sense: the safety of a man God holds, which is compatible with fear and trembling and never with carelessness. Zophar's “thou shalt be secure, because there is hope” is the right shape: security that rests on a ground outside the man, and knows it.
roots_summary: Hebrew batach (H982), to trust, be confident, be careless; betach (H983), security, carelessly; Greek amerimnos (G275), free from care.
roots_lines: Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, feel secure; Judges 18:7, 18:10, 18:27, Job 11:18, 12:6, Jeremiah 12:5.
Greek amerimnos (G275) — without care; Matthew 28:14, 1 Corinthians 7:32.
usage: “Quiet and secure… and there was no magistrate in the land” — Laish before the Danites.
“They that provoke God are secure” — the feeling and the fact opposite.
“Thou shalt be secure, because there is hope” — the right kind, grounded outside the man.

pos: v. and n. (to turn away, rebel, fall off from allegiance; rendering Hebrew sarah, sarar, and pasha)
etymology: Latin revolvere, to roll back, through Italian rivoltare. The Hebrew sarah is a turning aside, a defection.
biblical_def: Isaiah opens with it: “Why should ye be stricken any more? ye will revolt more and more: the whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint” (Isa 1:5); and confesses it: “In transgressing and lying against the LORD, and departing away from our God, speaking oppression and revolt” (Isa 59:13). The false prophet dies “because he hath spoken to turn you away from the LORD your God” — the margin, revolt against (Deu 13:5). Edom “revolted from under the hand of Judah” (2Ch 21:10; 2Ki 8:20). Jeremiah's people have “a revolting and a rebellious heart; they are revolted and gone” (Jer 5:23), and Israel has “deeply revolted” (Isa 31:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revolt as to fall off or turn from one's allegiance; to renounce obedience; to rebel; and, as a noun, desertion, change of sides.
webster_full: REVOLT, v.i. To fall off or turn from one to another.
2. To renounce allegiance and subjection to one's prince or state; to reject the authority of a sovereign; as a province or people revolting.
REVOLT, n. Desertion; change of sides; more properly, a renunciation of allegiance and subjection to one's prince or government.
scriptures: Isa 1:5
Why should ye be stricken any more? ye will revolt more and more: the whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint.
In transgressing and lying against the LORD, and departing away from our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering from the heart words of falsehood.
Jer 5:23
But this people hath a revolting and a rebellious heart; they are revolted and gone.
Isa 31:6
Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted.
So the Edomites revolted from under the hand of Judah unto this day. The same time also did Libnah revolt from under his hand; because he had forsaken the LORD God of his fathers.
corruption_summary: Rebellion is romanced as courage, and Isaiah's revolters were a nation already beaten to the bone and reaching for more.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 1:5 is the physiology of a revolt against God. The nation has been stricken until there is no sound place left — from the sole of the foot to the head, wounds and bruises and putrifying sores — and the prophet's question is not why they rebel but why they want more of the same: why should ye be stricken any more? ye will revolt more and more. Revolt against God is not the brave refusal of the modern imagination; it is a beaten body asking for the next blow. Jeremiah's diagnosis is the same organ: a revolting and a rebellious heart, and the two adjectives are one condition. Isaiah 31:6 gives the only cure the chapter knows — “Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted” — the same verb reversed, and the depth of the revolt made the measure of the return.
roots_summary: Hebrew sarah (H5627), a turning aside, defection, revolt; sarar (H5637), to be stubborn, rebellious; pasha (H6586), to rebel, break away; amaq (H6009), to be deep.
roots_lines: Hebrew sarah (H5627) — defection, revolt; Isaiah 1:5, 59:13, Deuteronomy 13:5, Jeremiah 28:16.
Hebrew sarar (H5637) — to be stubborn, revolting; Jeremiah 5:23, 6:28; pasha (H6586), to rebel, revolt; 2 Kings 8:20, 8:22, 2 Chronicles 21:8, 21:10.
Hebrew amaq (H6009) — to be deep, deeply revolted; Isaiah 31:6.
usage: “Why should ye be stricken any more? ye will revolt more and more” — a beaten body asking for the next blow.
“A revolting and a rebellious heart” — one organ, two adjectives.
“Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted” — the verb reversed.

pos: adj. (uneven, harsh, hairy, violent; rendering Hebrew rekes, eythan, sa'ar, and qashah, Greek trachus)
etymology: Old English rūh, hairy, shaggy; the sense of unevenness came from the feel of hair under the hand. The AV's rough garment is literally a hairy one.
biblical_def: Isaiah's highway for God: “the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain” (Isa 40:4), which the Baptist fulfilled — “the rough ways shall be made smooth” (Luk 3:5). In Daniel's vision “the rough goat is the king of Grecia” (Dan 8:21). Zechariah's false prophets shall no longer “wear a rough garment to deceive” (Zec 13:4). The heifer for an unsolved murder is brought “unto a rough valley, which is neither eared nor sown” (Deu 21:4). And of God's measured chastening: “he stayeth his rough wind in the day of the east wind” (Isa 27:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rough as having inequalities on the surface; not smooth; harsh; severe; coarse; tempestuous; hairy, shaggy.
webster_full: ROUGH, a. Having inequalities, small ridges or points on the surface; not smooth or plane; as a rough board; a rough stone.
2. Stormy; boisterous; tempestuous; as rough weather.
3. Harsh; severe; uncivil; rude; as a rough temper.
4. Hairy; shaggy; as a rough garment.
scriptures: Isa 40:4
Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:
Luk 3:5
Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth;
Dan 8:21
And the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.
Zec 13:4
And it shall come to pass in that day, that the prophets shall be ashamed every one of his vision, when he hath prophesied; neither shall they wear a rough garment to deceive:
Deu 21:4
And the elders of that city shall bring down the heifer unto a rough valley, which is neither eared nor sown, and shall strike off the heifer's neck there in the valley:
Isa 27:8
In measure, when it shooteth forth, thou wilt debate with it: he stayeth his rough wind in the day of the east wind.
corruption_summary: The rough garment is worn to look like a prophet, and Zechariah says the day is coming when no one will dare put it on.
corruption_paragraphs: Elijah wore hair and John wore camel's hair, and by Zechariah's day the costume had become the credential: a rough garment to deceive. The hair shirt, the studied severity, the rasp in the voice — every generation has men who put on the prophet's coat because it is easier than carrying the prophet's word, and Zechariah 13 foresees a day when the false prophets will be ashamed of their visions and disown the garment. Roughness is not holiness. Isaiah 40:4 uses the word the other way, for the ground the King will travel: the rough places plain, the crooked straight — the levelling that John preached as repentance, so that when the Lord came there would be no ridge of pride or pit of sin in the road. The roughness God wants removed is in the heart, and the roughness men put on is on the back.
roots_summary: Hebrew rekes (H7406), rough, rugged ground; eythan (H386), perennial, ever-flowing, rough; sa'ar (H8181), hair, hairy; sa'ir (H8163), a he-goat, shaggy; qashah (H7186), hard, rough; Greek trachus (G5138), rough.
roots_lines: Hebrew rekes (H7406) — rough, rugged; Isaiah 40:4 only; qashah (H7186), Isaiah 27:8.
Hebrew sa'ar (H8181) — hair, a hairy mantle; Zechariah 13:4, Genesis 25:25; sa'ir (H8163), the rough goat; Daniel 8:21; eythan (H386), Deuteronomy 21:4.
Greek trachus (G5138) — rough, rocky; Luke 3:5, Acts 27:29.
usage: “The rough places plain” — the road levelled for the King.
“Wear a rough garment to deceive” — the costume as credential.
“The rough goat is the king of Grecia” — prophecy's precision.

pos: v. (carried away with delight, enraptured; also, in the AV's darker sense, violated; rendering Hebrew labab, shagah, and shagal)
etymology: Old French ravir, from Latin rapere, to seize. English kept both directions of the seizing: to be ravished is to be carried off by delight, or carried off by force, and the Authorized Version has both.
biblical_def: The Bridegroom of the Song: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck” (Sng 4:9). Solomon to his son on marriage: “let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love. And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?” (Pro 5:19–20). The other sense is judgment: Babylon's “wives ravished” (Isa 13:16); “They ravished the women in Zion” (Lam 5:11); Jerusalem's “women ravished” in the day of the LORD (Zec 14:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ravish as to seize and carry away by violence; to have carnal knowledge of a woman by force; and, to transport with joy or delight.
webster_full: RAVISH, v.t. To seize and carry away by violence.
2. To have carnal knowledge of a woman by force and against her consent.
3. To bear away with joy or delight; to delight to ecstasy; to transport.
scriptures: Sng 4:9
Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.
Pro 5:19
Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.
Pro 5:20
And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?
Lam 5:11
They ravished the women in Zion, and the maids in the cities of Judah.
Their children also shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be spoiled, and their wives ravished.
corruption_summary: The word's violent sense has swallowed its delighted one, and Proverbs 5 commands a husband to be ravished with his wife.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern English has left the word only its crime, and the loss is theological. Proverbs 5:19 commands a man to be ravished always with his wife's love — carried away, intoxicated, the Hebrew is to reel — and the next verse asks why he would be ravished with a stranger instead. The marriage bed is not tolerated by Scripture as a concession; it is appointed as the place a man is meant to lose his head. The Song goes further and puts the word in the Bridegroom's mouth: thou hast ravished my heart — the Hebrew verb is made from the word for heart, as if to say, thou hast hearted me — with one glance. The church has always read that Bridegroom as Christ, and the sentence is then the most astonishing in the Bible: the delight runs from Him to her. Lamentations 5:11 shows the AV knew the other meaning and used it where it belonged, in a judgment; it is the modern reader who can no longer hear the difference.
roots_summary: Hebrew labab (H3823), to ravish the heart, to hearten; shagah (H7686), to reel, be intoxicated, go astray; shagal (H7693), to violate; anah (H6031), to humble, force.
roots_lines: Hebrew labab, piel (H3823) — to ravish the heart; Song of Solomon 4:9 only.
Hebrew shagah (H7686) — to reel, be carried away; Proverbs 5:19–20, 5:23, 20:1.
Hebrew shagal (H7693) — to violate; Isaiah 13:16, Zechariah 14:2; anah (H6031), Lamentations 5:11.
usage: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse” — the Bridegroom carried away by one glance.
“Be thou ravished always with her love” — the marriage bed as the appointed intoxication.
“They ravished the women in Zion” — the other sense, where it belongs.

pos: adv. (unjustly, without cause; rendering Hebrew sheqer, chamas, and belo mishpat, Greek adikos)
etymology: Wrong + ful + ly. The commonest Hebrew behind it, sheqer, is the word for a lie: to hate a man wrongfully is to hate him on a falsehood.
biblical_def: Peter: “this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully” (1Pe 2:19). David, in the psalm the Lord applied to Himself: “They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head: they that would destroy me, being mine enemies wrongfully, are mighty” (Psa 69:4). “Let not them that are mine enemies wrongfully rejoice over me” (Psa 35:19); “they that hate me wrongfully are multiplied” (Psa 38:19); “they persecute me wrongfully; help thou me” (Psa 119:86). Job: “the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me” (Job 21:27). Ezekiel: the people “have oppressed the stranger wrongfully” (Eze 22:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wrongfully as unjustly; in a manner contrary to the moral law or to justice.
webster_full: WRONGFULLY, adv. Unjustly; in a manner contrary to the moral law or to justice; as, to accuse one wrongfully; to suffer wrongfully.
scriptures: For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.
Psa 69:4
They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head: they that would destroy me, being mine enemies wrongfully, are mighty: then I restored that which I took not away.
Let not them that are mine enemies wrongfully rejoice over me: neither let them wink with the eye that hate me without a cause.
All thy commandments are faithful: they persecute me wrongfully; help thou me.
Behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me.
The people of the land have used oppression, and exercised robbery, and have vexed the poor and needy: yea, they have oppressed the stranger wrongfully.
corruption_summary: Suffering wrongfully is treated as an injustice to be corrected at once, and Peter calls it thankworthy and points to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: First Peter 2:19 was written to servants under masters who were not good and gentle but froward, and its counsel is the one the age cannot hear: to endure grief, suffering wrongfully, for conscience toward God, is thankworthy — grace, in the Greek. The demand for immediate vindication feels like justice and is usually pride, and Peter's argument in the next verses is Christ, who suffered wrongfully by every measure and “when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.” Psalm 69:4 is the same Christ from the other end: hated without a cause, wrongfully, and the Lord quoted the line of Himself in John 15:25. To be hated wrongfully is to stand where He stood. The other use of the word is the warning that the wronged do not become innocent by being wronged: Ezekiel 22:29 charges the same people who suffered under Babylon with having oppressed the stranger wrongfully at home.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheqer (H8267), a lie, falsehood, without cause; chamas (H2554), to do violence; belo mishpat (H4941), without judgment; Greek adikos (G95), unjustly.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsely, without cause; Psalm 35:19, 38:19, 69:4, 119:86.
Hebrew chamas (H2554) — to do violence, wrong; Job 21:27; belo mishpat (H4941), without judgment; Ezekiel 22:29.
Greek adikos (G95) — unjustly, wrongfully; 1 Peter 2:19 only.
usage: “Endure grief, suffering wrongfully” — thankworthy, because Christ did.
“Mine enemies wrongfully, are mighty” — the psalm the Lord quoted of Himself.
“Oppressed the stranger wrongfully” — the wronged are not thereby innocent.
